blocks.text: It is proved that חולד choled is not the weasel, as they hold, but the mole. Other names of the mole.

Levit. XI, 29. The Hebrew חלד choled the Greeks render γαλῆν [galēn], and Jerome mustela [weasel] [col. 1022]; Jonathan renders it כרכושתא carcoustha, and the Syriac ܟܟܘܫܬܐ cacaustho, which is the very same thing ^{(1)}. In Hesychius, indeed, κέρκος [kerkos] is ἀρουραῖος μῦς [arouraios mys], field mouse. [II, 436] And I once suspected that כרכושתא carcoustha was derived from κέρκος [kerkos], with the same meaning. But that כרכושתא carcoustha is an animal somewhat like the cat is proved by the Talmudic proverb in Sanhedrin ch. 2, fol. 85. 1: כרכושתא ושונרא עבדו הלולא מחרבא דבישא גדא, "When the carcoustha and the cat make a wedding, he who had been unfortunate lifts himself up." And that it is the weasel is clear from the fact that in Psal. CXIII, 9. the Hebrew words עקרת הבית, the barren woman of the house, are rendered thus, on the testimony of Elias, in some copies of the Chaldee Paraphrase: דיתבא מוריקא לאינשי ביתה היך כרכושתא דיתבא מדורא בעקרי ביתא, "She who sits pale before the men of her house, like the carcoustha, which sets its dwelling in the foundations of the house." As if עקרת in that place did not mean barren, but she who out of grief dwells בעקרי in the foundations, that is, in the lowest part of the house, as the carcoustha is wont to do. That this fits the description of the κατοικιδίου [katoikidiou] [domestic] weasel will be evident from what follows. Therefore, since חולד choled in Moses is the weasel, according to the opinion of so many ancients, all the Hebrews will seem to follow this with good reason: Baal Aruch, R. Solomon, Kimchi, Pomarius, Aquinas; and the more recent interpreters of Scripture, Pagninus, Arias, Castellio, Junius, Tremellius, etc.; also the vernacular ones, as many as I have been able to see, namely the French, Italian, English, Dutch, German. Not to mention the lexicographers, of whom there is none, as far as I know, who renders חולד choled otherwise than as weasel, or martes [marten], which is a species of weasel. And the Hebrew paraphrast of Aristeas, who renders these Greek words, Κακοποιητικὸς γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ, καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos gar ho tropos esti, kai galēs, kai myōn], into Hebrew thus:

[II, 437] כי הנה החולד והעכבר הם בטבעם דורכים אל ההשחתה ומועדים תמיד להרע, "For behold, the choled and the achbar (that is, the weasel and the mouse) by their nature tend toward destruction, and are always inclined to evil."

Yet I have reasons to doubt whether this is the true rendering. The first of them is that the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ chuldo, plainly formed from it, means the mole, not the weasel. So Giovanni Battista Ferrari and Thomas a Novaria determine in their Lexicons, or Syriac Nomenclators, published at Rome in the years 1622 and 1636 ^{(2)}. And this is confirmed by the most learned of the Maronites, Gabriel Sionita, who rendered the words of the Syriac translator in Proverb. XXIV, 31., ܘܚܦܝܘ ܐܦܘܗܝ ܚܘܠܕܐ, into Latin thus: And moles covered its surface. Nor indeed does the passage allow weasels to be understood. For it concerns the field of a lazy man, which is so neglected that nettles cover it. Nettles, that is, חרלים, is what stands in the Hebrew. But the Syriac read חלדים, the letter Resh being moved from its place and changed into Daleth, because the letters are similar; and accordingly he rendered ܚܘܠܕܐ ^{(3)}. That this word signifies not weasels but moles the matter itself shows. For a neglected field does not swarm with weasels, but it can swarm with moles, as the greatest Poet teaches in book 1 of the Georgics:
— — — — often the tiny mouse has set up its home beneath the ground and built its granaries; or blinded moles have dug their chambers.

This is the greatest bane of a field. Hence Simocatta in his Epistles: Τί δῆτα περὶ τῶν ἀσπαλάκων λέξαιμι, φοβερὸν γὰρ τῷ γεωργῷ τὸ κακὸν, καὶ δυσανταγώνιστον τὸ πολέμιον [Ti dēta peri tōn aspalakōn lexaimi, phoberon gar tō geōrgō to kakon, kai dysantagōniston to polemion]. What then shall I say about moles? For to the ploughman this [col. 1023] evil is terrible, and the enemy not easily overcome. Accordingly Stesimbrotus fabled that this animal ὑπὸ τῆς Γῆς τυφλωθῆναι, διὰ τὸ φθείρειν τοὺς καρποὺς [hypo tēs Gēs typhlōthēnai, dia to phtheirein tous karpous], had been blinded by Earth, because it ruined the crops. So Suidas and Apostolius under Τυφλότερος ἀσπάλακος [Typhloteros aspalakos].
